HREFLANG RECIPROCITY CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Do your hreflang alternates actually link back?

Paste a page's HTML and check its <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/"> tags for the misconfigurations Google's own hreflang documentation names directly: a missing reciprocal link back from the alternate page, an invalid or malformed language/region code (en-uk is not valid — the correct code is en-GB), a missing x-default fallback, a missing self-reference, and duplicate or conflicting hreflang values.

Nothing is uploaded. The HTML you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device — see "Why can't the browser just check this itself?" below for what an automatic-fetch attempt can and can't do.

1. Check a page

2. hreflang tags found on this page

hreflanghrefCode

No <link rel="alternate" hreflang="..."> tags found on this page.

Findings

Reciprocity — does each alternate link back?

This needs the alternate page's own HTML. Click "Try automatic fetch" first — it works when the target site allows cross-origin reads; most don't (see the FAQ), so paste the page's HTML manually when it fails.

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

The CLI fetches the page and every alternate it names over real HTTP — no cross-origin restriction, because it isn't a browser:

node check.mjs https://example.com/en/ --json
node check.mjs https://example.com/en/ --timeout 15000
node check.mjs https://example.com/en/ --max-alternates 20

Get check.mjs, fetch-page.mjs, and engine.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the target URL and the alternate hrefs that page's own tags name — nothing goes through this site. Exit code 1 when a danger-severity finding is produced, the target can't be fetched, or an alternate can't be fetched (unverified reciprocity is not the same as confirmed-clean).

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverity
ReciprocityPage A links to page B with hreflang, but B has no hreflang link back to ADanger
Invalid codeLanguage subtag not in ISO 639-1, or region subtag not in ISO 3166-1 (e.g. en-uk)Danger
Non-canonical casingA validly-coded tag written with the wrong case, e.g. EN-us instead of en-USNotice
Missing x-defaultTwo or more language/region variants declared, no hreflang="x-default" fallbackNotice
Missing self-referenceA page with hreflang tags does not include itself among its own alternatesDanger
Duplicate / conflictingThe same hreflang value declared twice — once harmlessly (same URL) and once dangerously (different URLs)Notice / Danger

Only the two-part language[-region] shape is validated against the full ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 lists. A script subtag (zh-Hans-CN) or a numeric UN M49 region (en-419) is recognized but not further validated — named as unvalidated rather than guessed at. More: why Google requires hreflang reciprocity, and the most common ways it breaks. See also: how this differs from Merkle's hreflang Tags Testing Tool, and this tool vs. checking hreflang tags by hand.

Common questions

What does "hreflang reciprocity" mean?

Google's Search Central documentation for hreflang says the links have to be reciprocal: if page A has a link rel=alternate hreflang tag pointing at page B, page B must have a matching tag pointing back at page A. If the return link is missing, Google's documentation says the annotation may be ignored — so a one-way hreflang link on a page you don't control the alternate for is effectively invisible to Google.

Why is en-uk invalid? It looks correct.

hreflang region subtags are ISO 3166-1 country codes, and "UK" was never assigned one — the United Kingdom's actual ISO 3166-1 code is "GB", inherited from its formal name (Great Britain and Northern Ireland). The correct tag is en-GB. This is one of the most common real-world hreflang mistakes because "UK" is the everyday abbreviation everyone actually uses.

Why can't the browser page just fetch the other language pages itself?

It tries to, but most sites will refuse to let a page running on a different origin read the response: unless the target server sends an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header naming this tool's origin (or *), the browser's Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policy blocks the page from reading what came back, even though the request itself often reaches the server. That is not a bug in this tool, it is the same origin-isolation protection that stops any website from silently reading another site's pages on your behalf. When a fetch is blocked this way, paste that page's HTML manually and the check runs exactly the same way. The zero-dependency CLI has no such restriction because it is not a browser tab.

Is this a full SEO audit?

No. It checks five specific, well-documented hreflang misconfigurations from Google's own documentation — reciprocity, code validity, x-default, self-reference, and duplicate/conflicting values. It is not a ranking guarantee, not a crawl of your whole site, and not a determination that your international SEO is otherwise correct.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not SEO, legal, or marketing advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It reports whether the hreflang tags on the page(s) you provided satisfy five specific, mechanically checkable rules — nothing more. It is not a ranking guarantee and not a substitute for Google Search Console's own International Targeting report. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. When you click "Try automatic fetch", this page makes a request directly from your browser to the URL shown — the same as opening it in a tab — and reads the response only if the target allows it; nothing about that request goes through this site either. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over the same page: Canonical Tag Checker checks which URL a page's own rel=canonical link names as authoritative — a different <link>-tag correctness question on the same head section. Structured Data Drift Check checks whether a page's JSON-LD still says what its visible text says. Social Preview Checker checks the Open Graph/Twitter Card tags a shared link renders as.

Free and open source. If this caught a broken alternate before Google did, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-hreflang-tags-by-hand.html.text:
← hreflang Reciprocity Check

hreflang Reciprocity Check vs. checking hreflang tags by hand

Reading a page's <link rel="alternate" hreflang> tags yourself is free and takes thirty seconds. It also cannot catch the two failures that break hreflang most often: a region code that looks right but was never assigned, and a reciprocal link that only fails to exist on a page you did not open.

What each approach is for

Checking by hand is fine for confirming a tag exists and is roughly the right shape — you will spot a missing href or an obviously mistyped attribute immediately. It cannot validate a region code against the actual ISO 3166-1 list from memory, and it cannot confirm reciprocity without opening every alternate page named on the one you started with and checking each one links back.

This tool validates every hreflang value's language and region subtags against the real BCP 47 / ISO 3166-1 data, checks that no two tags declare the same code for different URLs, flags a missing self-reference or x-default, and — given the alternate pages' content, either fetched by the CLI or pasted into the browser page — confirms each alternate actually links back. It runs free, with no account, and the browser page sends nothing to a server.

What checking by hand catchesWhat this tool catches too
A tag with no href, or an obviously misspelled attribute.Same, plus every hreflang value validated against the real language/region tables.
"en-uk" looks like a reasonable code for British English.Flags it: "UK" was never assigned an ISO 3166-1 region code; the real one is "GB".
Whether the page you are reading lists itself among its own alternates — if you think to check.Always checks self-reference, mechanically, on every run.
Whether every alternate page links back — only if you open all of them and compare by hand.Confirms reciprocity for every alternate given its content, and reports "unverified" rather than guessing when content isn't available.
Two same-code tags pointing at different URLs, if you notice the duplicate on the same page.Always flags conflicting or duplicate hreflang codes.

A hreflang set that looks complete

Four languages, four tags, every one present and syntactically well-formed:

hreflanghrefLooks right?
en/en/Yes
en-uk/en-uk/Yes, at a glance
fr/fr/Yes
es/es/Yes

Running this exact set through this tool's own engine reports:

FindingSeverityVisible by reading the /en/ page alone?
"en-uk" is not a valid hreflang value — "UK" was never assigned an ISO 3166-1 region code (the real one is "GB").DangerNo — the tag is syntactically well-formed.
The /es/ page does not link back to /en/, so the annotation is not reciprocal.DangerNo — requires opening /es/ and comparing its own tags.
No x-default declared for 4 language variants.NoticeOnly if you happen to know to look for it.

2 danger-level findings, 1 notice, from a set that reads as complete on the page you'd actually be looking at. Google's hreflang documentation states that a non-reciprocal annotation may be ignored entirely for both pages in the pair, so the /en/–/es/ relationship in this example gets no hreflang benefit at all despite four tags that all look fine. Figures taken directly from this tool's own buildReport(), not invented.

Neither approach is wrong for what it does. A quick read catches an obviously broken tag; it was never going to catch a plausible-looking invalid code or a link-back on a page you didn't open. This tool checks the parts that require comparing every value against a reference table and every alternate against every other alternate — the part manual review runs out of attention for first.

Common questions

Why is checking hreflang tags by eye unreliable?

Because the two failures that matter most are invisible from reading one page's markup. An invalid region code like "en-uk" is syntactically well-formed and reads as correct — "UK" looks like the obvious abbreviation for the United Kingdom, but ISO 3166-1 never assigned it a country code; the real one is "GB". And reciprocity failures require opening every alternate page and checking that each one links back, which does not show up from reading the page you started on.

What does a manual review usually catch, and what does it miss?

A human reviewer catches an obviously malformed tag — a missing href, a typo in the attribute name — because those look wrong on sight. What gets missed is exactly what looks right: a region code that reads like it should be valid, and a link-back on a page nobody opened. Reciprocity in particular requires checking N-1 other pages for every page in the set, which nobody does by hand past two or three languages.

How big is the gap in practice?

In the worked example on this page, a 4-language hreflang set with every tag present and well-formed at a glance carries 2 danger-level findings once actually checked: an invalid "en-uk" code, and one alternate page that never links back, breaking reciprocity for that pair. Google's own documentation says a non-reciprocal annotation may be ignored entirely — meaning the page pair with the broken link-back gets no hreflang benefit at all, despite four tags that all looked fine.

Is reading the tags by hand ever enough?

For a two-page site where you personally maintain both pages and remember to update both at once, eyeballing them can work. It stops scaling the moment a third language, a redirect, or a second author enters the picture, because reciprocity is a claim about every other page in the set, not about the one you are looking at.

Does this tool fetch pages for me?

The Node CLI does, over real HTTP, which is why it can check reciprocity unattended in CI. The browser page cannot reliably fetch a different origin itself (cross-origin requests are usually blocked), so it checks reciprocity from HTML you paste in for each alternate — still mechanical, still exhaustive, just not automatic in the browser the way the CLI is.

Nothing here says or implies that checking hreflang tags by hand is a bad practice — it is the obvious first move, and it catches obviously broken tags immediately. This page describes the specific failures it structurally cannot catch, not a fault in anyone who does it.

Open hreflang Reciprocity Check and run it against your own pages.

No warranty. This free tool is not SEO, legal, or professional advice, and it does not guarantee search-engine behavior for any hreflang configuration. Verify findings against Google's own documentation and your actual search-engine results before relying on them.

Nothing leaves your browser in the browser page unless you choose to fetch an alternate URL yourself; pasted HTML is processed locally. The Node CLI makes real HTTP requests to the URLs you give it, which is expected and necessary for the reciprocity check.

vs-merkle-hreflang-tool.html.text:
← hreflang Reciprocity Check

hreflang Reciprocity Check vs. Merkle's hreflang Tags Testing Tool

Merkle's hreflang Tags Testing Tool, published at technicalseo.com, is a well-known free tool in the technical SEO community: paste a URL, and it fetches the page server-side and reports on its hreflang set, including reciprocity between the pages it finds. For checking a single live URL by hand, it is a solid, established choice with a track record in the field.

hreflang Reciprocity Check checks the same underlying things — reciprocity, valid ISO 639-1 / ISO 3166-1 codes, x-default, self-reference, duplicates — but ships as two different surfaces instead of one hosted page: a zero-dependency Node CLI that fetches a target and its alternates over real HTTP and can run unattended as a CI gate against your own build, and a browser page that works entirely from HTML you paste in, so a page that is not public yet (a staging build, a draft behind a login) can still be checked without ever handing its content to a third-party server.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have one live URL and want a quick hreflang report right now. Either tool answers this well. Merkle's needs no HTML pasted in since it fetches for you; this tool's browser page needs the page's HTML (paste it, or let it try an automatic fetch).
I want hreflang reciprocity checked automatically on every build, before it ships. hreflang Reciprocity Check's CLI — node check.mjs <url> exits non-zero on a finding, wireable into any CI as an ordinary step, with no account or hosted service in the loop.
The page isn't public yet (staging, a draft, behind a login) and I don't want to hand its HTML to a third-party server. hreflang Reciprocity Check's browser page — paste the HTML and it never leaves your device. A tool that fetches the URL itself can't check a page it can't reach or isn't meant to reach.
I want a second opinion, or to compare two tools' read of the same page. Run both. Two independent implementations of the same documented rule agreeing is stronger evidence than either alone.

Neither tool replaces the other for every case. A one-off check of a page that's already live is exactly what Merkle's hosted tool is built for. A repeatable, unattended check wired into a CI pipeline, or a check of a page that isn't public, is what this tool adds.

Common questions

Should I use hreflang Reciprocity Check or Merkle's hreflang Tags Testing Tool?

Both check the same underlying thing — hreflang reciprocity and code validity — and either is a reasonable choice for checking one URL by hand. Merkle's tool fetches the live URL itself, server-side, which is convenient for a one-off check and needs no HTML pasted in. hreflang Reciprocity Check adds two things Merkle's hosted tool does not: a zero-dependency Node CLI you can run unattended in your own CI against a build's output, and a browser mode that works entirely from HTML you paste in, with nothing sent anywhere, for a page that is not live yet or that you'd rather not point a third-party tool's server at.

Does Merkle's tool check reciprocity?

Yes — Merkle's hreflang Tags Testing Tool, published at technicalseo.com, is a well-known tool in the technical SEO community specifically for validating hreflang tags including whether alternates link back to each other, based on its own public documentation of what it checks.

Is Merkle's tool free?

Yes, based on its own public listing on technicalseo.com — no account is required to check a single URL. hreflang Reciprocity Check is also free, with no account, and the two are not competing on price — the difference is where the check runs and what you can automate with it.

Is this page affiliated with Merkle?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Merkle. Merkle and its hreflang Tags Testing Tool are named here only to describe what that tool does and how it differs from this one, based on Merkle's own public documentation.

More: why hreflang links must be reciprocal.

why-hreflang-must-be-reciprocal.html.text:
← hreflang Reciprocity Check

Why hreflang links must be reciprocal

Google's Search Central documentation on localized pages is direct about this: hreflang annotations describe a set of pages that are equivalent alternates of each other, and it asks site owners to confirm the links are reciprocal — every page in the set should link to every other page in the set, including itself. When a page names an alternate that does not link back, Google's own documentation says the annotation may be disregarded.

That is a quiet failure. The page still renders. The HTML is still valid. Nothing in a browser, a linter, or a normal QA pass will show a broken hreflang set — the only symptom is a search result that doesn't show up where it was supposed to, in a market nobody in the room is testing from.

The shape of a correct set

Three pages, each in a different language, each listing all three (including itself):

<!-- on https://example.com/en/ -->
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="de" href="https://example.com/de/" />

<!-- on https://example.com/fr/ -->
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="de" href="https://example.com/de/" />

<!-- on https://example.com/de/ -->
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="de" href="https://example.com/de/" />

Every page names all three, including itself (the self-reference Google's documentation also asks for). If the German page above were missing its own entry pointing back at /fr/, the French page's link to German would be one-way, and Google's documentation says it may be ignored for exactly that pair.

How a one-way link actually happens

Almost never on purpose. The common real cause is a rollout: a site adds a new locale and updates its language switcher and hreflang block for the new page, but the existing pages' hreflang blocks are generated from a template or a migration script that only ran once, before the new locale existed. Every existing page keeps pointing at the same set it always had; the new page points at all of them; nothing points back at the new page except the new page itself. The same thing happens in reverse when a locale is retired — its alternates keep naming a page that no longer exists or was never repointed.

The other four ways this tool checks for

  • Invalid codes. A region subtag that isn't a real ISO 3166-1 code — "UK" is the single most common instance, since it's the everyday abbreviation for a country whose actual code is "GB".
  • Missing x-default. Recommended, not required, for a page set with more than one real variant, as the fallback for a visitor who matches none of them.
  • Missing self-reference. A page that names alternates but never lists itself among them.
  • Duplicate or conflicting values. The same hreflang code pointing at two different URLs is a real conflict a search engine cannot resolve on your behalf; the same code pointing at the same URL twice is just redundant.

Common questions

Where does Google say hreflang links must be reciprocal?

Google's Search Central documentation on localized versions of a page instructs site owners to confirm that hreflang links are reciprocal — each page in a set of alternates should link to every other page, and every other page should link back to it. Google's own guidance says that when a return link is missing, the search engine may disregard the annotation.

What actually happens if the return link is missing?

Google's documentation says a hreflang annotation without a matching return link may be ignored. In practice this means the language- or region-targeted result you intended for a search in a particular market may not appear, and instead a visitor might land on the wrong-language version of the page with no signal ever reaching you that the annotation failed, because nothing about it produces an error — the page still loads fine and the tag is still valid HTML.

How does a one-way hreflang link happen in practice?

Usually a new locale is added to a site's language switcher and its hreflang set before every existing locale's own page has been updated to add a matching entry pointing at the new one — a rollout that touches N pages needs to touch N pages' hreflang blocks, and a template or migration script that only updates the new page's own tag leaves every existing page pointing at nothing that points back. It also happens when a page is retired or moved and its alternates are not updated to drop or repoint the now-dead entry.

What is x-default and is it required?

hreflang="x-default" names the page to show a visitor whose language or region does not match any of the other declared alternates. Google's documentation describes it as optional but recommended whenever a page set has more than one real language or region variant, specifically for sites that do automatic language/country selection with a landing page a generic visitor should see.

Check your own pages: hreflang Reciprocity Check. See also: how this differs from Merkle's hreflang Tags Testing Tool.
